Mercury.explanation: Mercury is the smallest planet and closest to the Sun with extreme temperature swings
points: Smallest planet in the Solar System – diameter only ~4,879 km
Closest planet to the Sun with an average distance of ~58 million km
Extreme temperature variation: up to ~430 °C on the day side, down to ~-180 °C at night
No substantial atmosphere – surface exposed directly to solar radiation and space
Has the shortest orbital period (year) of only 88 Earth days

Venus.explanation: Venus is the hottest planet at 465°C and spins backwards compared to most planets
points: Hottest planet in the Solar System with surface temperature averaging ~465 °C
Retrograde rotation – spins clockwise (opposite direction to most planets)
Very slow rotation: one day on Venus lasts longer than one year (~243 Earth days vs 225 Earth days)
Thick carbon dioxide atmosphere creates extreme greenhouse effect
Surface pressure ~92 times that of Earth – equivalent to being 900 m underwater

Earth.explanation: Earth is the only planet known to have life and liquid water on its surface
points: Only known astronomical object confirmed to harbor life
71% of surface covered by liquid water – unique in the inner Solar System
Has a strong magnetic field generated by molten iron-nickel core
Atmosphere rich in nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%) – supports complex life
Plate tectonics and active geology distinguish it from other rocky planets

Mars.explanation: Mars is called the Red Planet and has the largest volcano in the solar system
points: Iron oxide (rust) on surface gives characteristic red color
Olympus Mons – tallest known volcano and mountain in Solar System (~22 km high)
Has the longest canyon system (Valles Marineris) – over 4,000 km long
Thin atmosphere mostly carbon dioxide – surface pressure ~0.6% of Earth's
Evidence of ancient liquid water – dry river valleys, lakebeds, polar ice caps

Jupiter.explanation: Jupiter is the largest planet and its Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than Earth
points: Largest planet – diameter ~11 times Earth, mass ~318 times Earth
Great Red Spot – anticyclonic storm larger than Earth, active for at least 350 years
Strongest magnetic field of any planet – creates intense radiation belts
Shortest day – rotates once every ~10 hours (fastest rotation)
Has at least 95 known moons – including four large Galilean moons

Saturn.explanation: Saturn has beautiful rings made of ice and rock visible from Earth with a small telescope
points: Most prominent and complex ring system in the Solar System
Rings mostly composed of water ice particles with some rocky material
Least dense planet – average density lower than water (would float in a bathtub)
Has at least 146 known moons – including large moon Titan with thick atmosphere
Hexagonal storm pattern at north pole – unique atmospheric feature

Uranus.explanation: Uranus rotates on its side as if it was knocked over by a giant collision long ago
points: Extreme axial tilt of ~98° – essentially rolls on its side during orbit
Likely caused by massive collision early in Solar System history
Coldest planetary atmosphere – minimum temperature ~−224 °C
Faint ring system and 27 known moons (mostly named after Shakespeare characters)
Blue-green color from methane in atmosphere absorbing red light

Neptune.explanation: Neptune is the windiest planet with storms reaching speeds of 2100 km per hour
points: Strongest sustained winds of any planet – up to ~2,100 km/h
Deep blue color from methane absorption in atmosphere
Dynamic weather – Great Dark Spot storm observed by Voyager 2 in 1989
Strong internal heat source – radiates 2.6 times more heat than it receives
14 known moons – largest is Triton, which orbits retrograde

Pluto.explanation: Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 and has a heart-shaped nitrogen plain
points: Reclassified from planet to dwarf planet by IAU in 2006
Tombaugh Regio – large heart-shaped nitrogen ice plain on surface
Largest known trans-Neptunian object in Kuiper Belt
Has five moons – largest Charon is about half Pluto's size (binary system)
Thin nitrogen-methane atmosphere that freezes onto surface when farther from Sun

Ceres.explanation: Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter
points: Largest object in the asteroid belt – diameter ~940 km
Only dwarf planet in the inner Solar System
Bright spots (faculae) on surface – salt deposits from subsurface brine
Has water ice – possibly more fresh water than all of Earth's freshwater
Visited by Dawn spacecraft (2015–2018) – first dwarf planet orbited

Eris.explanation: Eris is a distant dwarf planet even slightly larger than Pluto
points: Most massive known dwarf planet – ~27% more massive than Pluto
Slightly larger diameter than Pluto (~2,326 km vs ~2,377 km)
Highly eccentric orbit – ranges from 38 to 97 AU from Sun
Has one moon – Dysnomia
Discovery (2005) triggered the redefinition of “planet”

Makemake.explanation: Makemake is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt named after a creation deity
points: Named after Rapa Nui (Easter Island) creator god
Second-brightest Kuiper Belt object after Pluto
Very low albedo before discovery of atmosphere – now known to have thin methane atmosphere
No known moons (as of 2025)
Highly elongated orbit – 310–490 years orbital period

Haumea.explanation: Haumea spins so fast it is squashed into an egg shape unlike any other body
points: Fastest-rotating large body in Solar System – ~4-hour day
Extreme elongation due to rapid spin – longest/shortest axes ratio ~2:1
Has two small moons – Hiʻiaka and Namaka
Ring system discovered in 2017 – first Kuiper Belt object with rings
Surface covered in crystalline water ice – unusually pure

Sedna.explanation: Sedna has an extremely elongated orbit taking over 11,000 years to go around the Sun
points: Most distant known object in Solar System with confirmed orbit (~84 AU average)
Extreme orbital period ~11,400 years – perihelion ~76 AU, aphelion ~937 AU
Reddish color – possibly due to tholins (organic compounds)
Possible inner Oort Cloud object or detached disk member
No known moons – very small (diameter ~1,000 km)

Quaoar.explanation: Quaoar is a Kuiper Belt object that surprisingly has its own ring system
points: First Kuiper Belt object found to have a ring system (2023)
Ring lies outside Roche limit – very unusual
Has one moon – Weywot
Diameter ~1,100–1,300 km – near hydrostatic equilibrium
Named after Tongva creator deity

Orcus.explanation: Orcus is sometimes called anti-Pluto because its orbit mirrors Pluto's almost exactly
points: Plutino – in 2:3 orbital resonance with Neptune like Pluto
Orbit almost exactly opposite Pluto – called “anti-Pluto”
Has one moon – Vanth
Surface rich in water ice and possibly ammonium compounds
Diameter ~900–1,000 km

Varuna.explanation: Varuna is a large trans-Neptunian object with a very fast rotation period
points: Very fast rotation – ~6.3 hour day
Elongated shape due to spin – not in hydrostatic equilibrium
Diameter ~600–700 km
Named after Hindu god of water and celestial ocean
One of the brightest classical Kuiper Belt objects

Ixion.explanation: Ixion is a plutino dwarf planet candidate in resonance with Neptune's orbit
points: Plutino – 2:3 resonance with Neptune
Reddish surface – likely tholins
Diameter ~710 km – possible dwarf planet
Named after Greek mythological figure punished in Tartarus
Among the largest plutinos after Pluto

Gonggong.explanation: Gonggong is a large red Kuiper Belt object with a small moon called Xiangliu
points: Very red surface – high concentration of tholins
Has one moon – Xiangliu (discovered 2010)
Diameter ~1,230 km – likely dwarf planet
Named after Chinese water god who caused great floods
Highly inclined and eccentric orbit

Planet Nine.explanation: Planet Nine is a hypothetical giant planet thought to be lurking unseen in the outer solar system
points: Hypothetical super-Earth or ice giant ~5–10 Earth masses
Proposed to explain clustering of extreme trans-Neptunian orbits
Predicted orbit: 400–800 AU from Sun, period 10,000–20,000 years
Not yet discovered – only indirect gravitational evidence
If real, would be the fifth-largest planet in Solar System

Hot Jupiter.explanation: Hot Jupiters are gas giant exoplanets orbiting very close to their stars incredibly fast
points: Gas giants orbiting extremely close to parent star (<0.05 AU)
Orbital periods typically 1–10 days – very hot surfaces
First type of exoplanet discovered around Sun-like stars (1995)
Many have dayside temperatures >1,000 °C
Often tidally locked – one side always faces star

Super Earth.explanation: Super Earths are rocky exoplanets larger than Earth but smaller than Neptune
points: Mass 1–10× Earth – radius 1.2–2.5× Earth
May be rocky, ocean worlds, or mini-Neptunes
Most common type of planet discovered by Kepler mission
Some lie in habitable zones of their stars
Can have very high gravity – up to several times Earth's

Ocean World.explanation: Ocean worlds are planets or moons entirely covered by deep global oceans
points: Planets/moons with global subsurface or surface oceans (often beneath ice)
Examples include Europa, Enceladus, Ganymede, Titan, and some exoplanets
Potential for life due to liquid water and possible chemical energy sources
Many are tidally heated by parent planet (e.g., Jupiter's moons)
Could have oceans hundreds of kilometers deep

Lava Planet.explanation: Lava worlds are exoplanets so close to their stars that the surface is molten rock
points: Rocky planets with dayside surface temperatures high enough to melt rock
Surface may be covered in magma oceans
Examples include CoRoT-7b, K2-141b, and 55 Cancri e
Extreme stellar irradiation strips atmospheres in many cases
Some may have lava “weather” – silicate vapor clouds and rain

Diamond Planet.explanation: Some exoplanets are thought to have interiors made largely of diamond-like carbon
points: High-pressure carbon planets where carbon crystallizes into diamond
55 Cancri e is the most famous candidate – may be carbon-rich
Formed from carbon-oxygen rich protoplanetary disks
Could have thick diamond layers beneath graphite or other forms
Very high density compared to Earth-like rocky planets

Rogue Planet.explanation: Rogue planets drift through space without any star to orbit, frozen and dark
points: Free-floating planets not bound to any star
Likely ejected from original planetary systems
Extremely cold surface temperatures (~−200 °C or lower)
Some may retain internal heat or have thick hydrogen atmospheres
Examples include PSO J318.5-22 and several microlensing discoveries

Water World.explanation: GJ 1214 b is a water world with a thick steamy atmosphere and possible deep ocean
points: GJ 1214 b – classic example of a water-rich mini-Neptune / super-Earth
Thick hydrogen-helium atmosphere with large water vapor component
Possible global ocean beneath atmosphere – hundreds of km deep
High surface pressure – water may be in exotic states (hot ice)
Temperature ~200–300 °C at cloud tops

Pulsar Planet.explanation: The first confirmed exoplanets ever found orbit a pulsar, a rapidly spinning dead star
points: PSR B1257+12 system – first confirmed exoplanets (1992)
Orbit millisecond pulsar – remnant of supernova
Planets likely formed from supernova debris disk
Extreme radiation environment – unlikely to host life
Three rocky planets detected via pulsar timing

Proxima b.explanation: Proxima Centauri b is the closest known exoplanet to Earth just 4 light-years away
points: Closest known exoplanet to our Solar System (~4.24 light-years)
Orbits in habitable zone of red dwarf Proxima Centauri
Mass ~1.17 Earth masses – likely rocky
Tidally locked – one side always faces star
Subject to strong stellar flares from its red dwarf host

Kepler-452b.explanation: Kepler-452b is often called Earth's cousin as it orbits a sun-like star in the habitable zone
points: Orbits G-type (Sun-like) star – very similar to our Sun
Receives ~10% more stellar energy than Earth
Radius ~1.6× Earth – likely rocky or mini-Neptune
Orbital period ~385 days – very Earth-like year
Age of system ~6 billion years – older than Solar System

TRAPPIST-1e.explanation: TRAPPIST-1e is one of seven Earth-sized planets orbiting an ultra-cool dwarf star
points: One of seven roughly Earth-sized planets in TRAPPIST-1 system
Receives similar amount of starlight as Earth from its star
Likely rocky – radius and mass suggest Earth-like density
Possibly tidally locked – extreme day/night temperature contrast
Prime target for JWST atmospheric studies

HD 189733b.explanation: HD 189733b is a vivid blue planet where it rains molten glass sideways in 8700 km/h winds
points: Deep blue color due to silicate particles in atmosphere
Extreme winds ~8,700 km/h – glass rain sideways
Hot Jupiter with dayside temperature ~1,200 °C
Sodium and water vapor detected in atmosphere
One of the first exoplanets with detailed atmospheric map

55 Cancri e.explanation: 55 Cancri e is a lava world that may have a surface of molten rock and carbon
points: Super-Earth / mini-Neptune with dayside ~2,400 °C
Likely covered in magma ocean
Possible carbon-rich composition – diamond layers theorized
Very short orbital period – 18 hours
Phase curve shows heat redistribution from dayside to nightside

HAT-P-7b.explanation: HAT-P-7b is a massive hot Jupiter where it rains rubies and sapphires
points: Albedo ~0.5 – highly reflective (shiny)
Possible corundum (aluminum oxide) clouds – ruby/sapphire rain
Dayside temperature ~2,200–2,800 °C
Strong thermal inversion in atmosphere
One of the brightest hot Jupiters observed

WASP-17b.explanation: WASP-17b is one of the largest known exoplanets with a density lower than balsa wood
points: One of the largest and lowest-density exoplanets known
Radius ~1.99 Jupiter radii, mass ~0.49 Jupiter masses
Very inflated – extremely low density (~0.19 g/cm³)
Hot Jupiter with 3.7-day orbit
Retrograde orbit – likely result of dynamical interactions

GJ 436b.explanation: GJ 436b is a hot Neptune with a gigantic comet-like tail of hydrogen streaming from it
points: Warm Neptune losing atmosphere rapidly
Huge hydrogen tail – extends far behind planet
Mass loss rate ~1,000 tons per second
Helium detected in escaping atmosphere
Orbiting red dwarf star ~33 light-years away

Kepler-16b.explanation: Kepler-16b orbits two stars at once like the fictional Tatooine from Star Wars
points: First confirmed circumbinary planet – orbits two stars
Gas giant similar to Saturn in mass
Stable orbit around binary star pair
Orbital period ~229 days
Popularly called “Tatooine planet”

PSR B1257+12 b.explanation: PSR B1257+12 b was the very first exoplanet ever confirmed, discovered in 1992
points: First confirmed exoplanet (1992) – predates 51 Peg b
Orbits millisecond pulsar PSR B1257+12
Rocky planet ~0.02 Earth masses
Extreme radiation environment from pulsar
Part of first multi-planet system discovered

Tau Ceti e.explanation: Tau Ceti e is a super Earth orbiting a sun-like star just 12 light-years away
points: Super-Earth orbiting nearby Sun-like star (~11.9 light-years)
Mass ~4.3–6.7 Earth masses
Close orbit – receives more energy than Venus
One of the nearest potentially rocky exoplanets
Still debated whether rocky or gaseous

Wolf 1061c.explanation: Wolf 1061c is one of the closest potentially habitable exoplanets at 14 light-years
points: Orbits in conservative habitable zone of red dwarf Wolf 1061
Mass ~4 Earth masses – likely rocky
Distance ~14 light-years – one of the nearest habitable-zone candidates
Orbital period ~17.9 days
Red dwarf host means potential tidal locking

Gliese 667Cc.explanation: Gliese 667Cc may be in the habitable zone of a triple star system
points: Orbits one component of triple red dwarf system
Mass ~3.8–4.5 Earth masses
Within habitable zone – receives ~90% of Earth's stellar energy
Potential rocky super-Earth
Triple star environment – complex seasonal effects possible

K2-18b.explanation: K2-18b may have a hydrogen-rich atmosphere and possible ocean beneath
points: Hycean candidate – possible hydrogen atmosphere + global ocean
Radius ~2.6× Earth, mass ~8.6× Earth
Water vapor and methane detected in atmosphere
Orbital period ~33 days around red dwarf
Prime target for JWST habitability studies

LHS 1140b.explanation: LHS 1140b is a rocky super Earth in the habitable zone with a thick atmosphere
points: Dense rocky planet – mass ~6.5 Earth masses, radius ~1.7 Earth radii
Receives similar stellar energy as Earth
Likely retains thick atmosphere despite red dwarf host
Strong candidate for liquid water surface
One of the best targets for atmospheric characterization

TOI 700d.explanation: TOI 700d is a nearby Earth-sized planet in the habitable zone of a small red star
points: Earth-sized planet (~1.1–1.2 Earth radii)
Orbits in habitable zone of quiet red dwarf TOI 700
Distance ~101 light-years
Likely rocky – prime target for JWST
One of the first Earth-sized habitable-zone planets found by TESS

Ross 128b.explanation: Ross 128b is a temperate Earth-mass planet orbiting a quiet red dwarf star
points: Mass ~1.4–1.8 Earth masses – likely rocky
Receives ~1.38× Earth's stellar flux
Orbits very quiet red dwarf – low flare activity
Distance ~11 light-years – one of the closest temperate planets
Potential for liquid water on surface

Teegarden b.explanation: Teegarden b receives similar energy from its star as Earth does from the Sun
points: Mass ~1.05 Earth masses – very Earth-like
Stellar flux almost identical to Earth's (~1.15×)
Orbits very quiet red dwarf Teegarden's Star
Distance ~12.5 light-years
High Earth Similarity Index – one of the most Earth-like candidates

LP 890-9c.explanation: LP 890-9c is one of the most promising habitable zone rocky planets found to date
points: Radius ~1.37× Earth, mass ~2–8 Earth masses (estimated)
Receives ~1.0–1.2× Earth's stellar energy
Orbits quiet red dwarf LP 890-9
Very promising for follow-up observations
Part of SPECULOOS discovery – two temperate planets in system

Barnard b.explanation: A planet candidate was reported around Barnard's Star just 6 light-years from Earth
points: Candidate super-Earth around nearest solitary red dwarf (~6 light-years)
Mass ~0.4 Earth masses (if real)
Cold orbit – receives ~2–3% of Earth's stellar energy
Discovery via radial velocity – still debated
If confirmed, one of the closest exoplanets

OGLE-2005-BLG.explanation: OGLE microlensing planets are discovered when their gravity bends distant starlight
points: OGLE-2005-BLG-390Lb – first cold rocky exoplanet found via microlensing
Mass ~5.5 Earth masses
Very distant orbit – ~5 AU from host star
Technique detects planets down to Earth mass at large distances
Host star likely red dwarf or brown dwarf

HR 8799b.explanation: HR 8799b was one of the first exoplanets to be directly photographed in visible light
points: One of the first directly imaged exoplanets (2008)
Gas giant ~7 Jupiter masses
Orbits at ~68 AU from young A-type star
Bright in infrared – still forming and glowing from heat
Part of four-planet directly imaged system

Beta Pic b.explanation: Beta Pictoris b was photographed orbiting inside a visible debris disk around its star
points: First exoplanet directly imaged inside a debris disk (2008)
Gas giant ~8–15 Jupiter masses
Orbits at ~9 AU from young A-type star
Still forming – very hot (~1,300 °C)
Helps study planet formation in real time

Fomalhaut b.explanation: Fomalhaut b was photographed near a striking ring-shaped debris disk
points: First exoplanet directly imaged near debris disk (2008)
Very large orbit (~115 AU)
Later observations suggest it may be a dust cloud or evaporating protoplanet
Star Fomalhaut is bright and nearby (~25 light-years)
Helped understand planet-disk interactions

HIP 65426b.explanation: HIP 65426b was the first exoplanet directly imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
points: First planet directly imaged by JWST (2022)
Gas giant ~6–12 Jupiter masses
Orbits at ~100 AU from young A-type star
Very hot – still glowing from formation
Important for JWST exoplanet imaging calibration

Qatar-1b.explanation: Qatar-1b was one of the first exoplanets discovered through the Qatar Exoplanet Survey
points: Hot Jupiter discovered by Qatar Exoplanet Survey (2010)
Orbital period ~1.42 days
Radius ~1.16 Jupiter radii, mass ~1.33 Jupiter masses
Orbiting K-type star
One of the earliest discoveries from Middle Eastern astronomy programs

KELT-9b.explanation: KELT-9b is the hottest known exoplanet at over 4,000 degrees, hotter than most stars
points: Hottest known exoplanet – dayside ~4,300 °C
Hotter than most stars – molecules dissociate on dayside
Hot Jupiter orbiting hot A-type star
Very short orbit – 1.48 days
Atmosphere may contain atomic iron and titanium

WASP-96b.explanation: WASP-96b's atmosphere was analyzed by James Webb revealing water vapor and clouds
points: First exoplanet atmosphere spectrum published by JWST (2022)
Clear detection of water vapor
Evidence of clouds and possible haze
Hot Saturn-sized planet with 3.2-day orbit
Important benchmark for JWST transmission spectroscopy

WASP-121b.explanation: WASP-121b has iron and titanium vapor in its upper atmosphere detected by spectroscopy
points: Hot Jupiter with strong atmospheric escape
Atomic iron, titanium, and vanadium detected in upper atmosphere
Dayside temperature ~2,500–3,000 °C
Heavy metals vaporized and present in gas phase
One of the best-studied ultra-hot Jupiters

LTT 9779b.explanation: LTT 9779b has a metallic atmosphere and reflects 80% of starlight making it highly shiny
points: Highest albedo known for hot Neptune (~0.8)
Metallic clouds likely cause high reflectivity
Very short orbit – 0.79 days
Dayside temperature ~2,000 °C
Transition object between hot Jupiter and ultra-hot Neptune

COCONUTS-2b.explanation: COCONUTS-2b is the coldest and closest directly-imaged exoplanet to Earth known
points: Coldest directly imaged exoplanet – ~160–190 K
Very wide orbit (~6,400 AU)
Mass ~6 Jupiter masses
Distance to Earth ~35 light-years (closest imaged planet)
Likely formed by gravitational collapse

Luhman 16.explanation: Luhman 16 is the closest brown dwarf system just 6.5 light-years from Earth
points: Third-closest system to Earth (~6.5 light-years)
Binary brown dwarfs (Luhman 16A and 16B)
No confirmed planets yet, but excellent target for future searches
Very cool temperatures – ~1,200–1,500 K
Discovered via WISE telescope (2013)

WD 1856b.explanation: WD 1856b orbits a white dwarf star having somehow survived the star's red giant phase
points: Jupiter-sized planet orbiting white dwarf at ~0.02 AU
Survived host star's red giant phase without being engulfed
Likely migrated inward after star became white dwarf
Very cold planet now (~200 K)
First planet confirmed to orbit white dwarf

TOI-1231b.explanation: TOI-1231b is a Neptune-sized exoplanet that may have water clouds in its atmosphere
points: Sub-Neptune / mini-Neptune with radius ~3.5× Earth
Temperature ~330 K – cool enough for water clouds
Orbiting quiet M dwarf ~90 light-years away
One of the best targets for JWST transmission spectroscopy
Possible hazy or cloudy atmosphere

GJ 3470b.explanation: GJ 3470b is a warm Neptune losing its atmosphere to stellar radiation
points: Warm Neptune losing hydrogen envelope rapidly
Large escaping atmosphere detected via Lyman-alpha
Mass loss rate one of the highest observed
Orbiting red dwarf at ~0.03 AU
Transition object – may lose envelope completely

GJ 1132b.explanation: GJ 1132b may have rebuilt a secondary atmosphere from volcanic activity after losing its original
points: Rocky super-Earth ~1.6 Earth radii
Possible secondary atmosphere from volcanism
Original H/He envelope likely lost to stellar radiation
Orbiting red dwarf ~41 light-years away
Prime target for JWST to study rocky planet atmospheres

K2-141b.explanation: K2-141b is a lava world with a supersonic silicate wind blowing across its surface
points: Extreme lava planet – dayside ~2,000–3,000 °C
Supersonic winds carry vaporized rock from dayside to nightside
Possible mineral clouds and rock rain on cooler side
Very short orbit – 0.28 days
One of the most extreme rocky exoplanets known

Kepler-22b.explanation: Kepler-22b was the first confirmed exoplanet in the habitable zone of a sun-like star
points: First habitable-zone planet found by Kepler (2011)
Radius ~2.4× Earth – likely mini-Neptune or water world
Orbits G-type star similar to Sun
Receives ~80% of Earth's stellar flux
Orbital period ~290 days

Kepler-69c.explanation: Kepler-69c is a super Earth orbiting in the habitable zone of a sun-like star
points: Radius ~1.7× Earth – possible super-Venus or rocky
Receives ~2.3× Earth's stellar flux (hot side of HZ)
Orbits G-type star
Orbital period ~242 days
Early candidate for habitability studies

Kepler-62e.explanation: Kepler-62e could be a water world with a global ocean and no land
points: Super-Earth / mini-Neptune in habitable zone
Radius ~1.6× Earth
Likely ocean world or water-rich planet
Receives ~20% less stellar flux than Earth
Orbits K-type star – orbital period ~122 days

Kepler-186f.explanation: Kepler-186f was the first Earth-size exoplanet found in the habitable zone of any star
points: First Earth-sized planet in habitable zone (2014)
Radius ~1.1× Earth – likely rocky
Receives ~32% of Earth's stellar flux
Orbits red dwarf star
Orbital period ~130 days

Kepler-438b.explanation: Kepler-438b was once considered the most Earth-like exoplanet found with Earth Similarity Index of 0.88
points: Very high Earth Similarity Index (~0.88)
Radius ~1.12× Earth – likely rocky
Receives ~70% of Earth's stellar flux
Orbits red dwarf – potential tidal locking
High flare activity from host star may affect habitability

Kepler-442b.explanation: Kepler-442b orbits a star cooler than the Sun but still receives the right amount of energy
points: One of the most Earth-like planets by stellar flux received
Radius ~1.34× Earth
Receives ~66–70% of Earth's energy
Orbits K-type star – orbital period ~112 days
High Earth Similarity Index (~0.84–0.86)

Kepler-1649c.explanation: Kepler-1649c is one of the most Earth-sized and habitable zone matching planets found
points: Radius ~1.06× Earth – very close to Earth size
Receives ~75% of Earth's stellar flux
Orbits red dwarf star
Orbital period ~19.5 days
Re-analyzed from Kepler data – previously overlooked

TOI-700e.explanation: TOI-700e is an inner habitable zone planet discovered alongside its sibling TOI-700d
points: Earth-sized planet in inner habitable zone of TOI-700
Radius ~0.95× Earth
Receives slightly more energy than Earth
Part of three-planet system around quiet red dwarf
Excellent JWST target for atmospheric study

55 Cancri f.explanation: 55 Cancri f is a giant planet that orbits in its star's habitable zone
points: Gas giant / ice giant in habitable zone
Mass ~0.14–0.28 Jupiter masses
Receives Earth-like stellar flux
Orbits bright nearby star (~41 light-years)
Part of one of the closest multi-planet systems

Upsilon Andromedae d.explanation: Upsilon Andromedae d was one of the first multiplanet systems discovered around a normal star
points: Part of first multi-planet system around Sun-like star (1999)
Gas giant ~10 Jupiter masses
Wide orbit – ~2.5 AU
Stable despite eccentric companion planets
One of the earliest known Jupiter analogs

Pi Mensae c.explanation: Pi Mensae c is a super Earth orbiting a star just 60 light-years away
points: Super-Earth / mini-Neptune ~4.8 Earth masses
Orbital period ~6.3 days – very close orbit
Around nearby bright star (~59 light-years)
Possible atmosphere detectable
Host star has known long-period giant planet

L 98-59b.explanation: L 98-59b is one of the smallest exoplanets to have its atmosphere studied by JWST
points: Small rocky planet ~0.9 Earth radii
Very close orbit around red dwarf
JWST transmission spectrum obtained – one of the smallest targets
Possible thin atmosphere or bare rock
Part of multi-planet system

TRAPPIST-1f.explanation: TRAPPIST-1f is one of the most studied exoplanets and a prime target for habitability research
points: One of seven Earth-sized planets in TRAPPIST-1 system
Outer habitable-zone planet – cooler side
Likely rocky or water-rich
Extensive JWST observations ongoing
Possible tidal heating from resonances

TRAPPIST-1g.explanation: TRAPPIST-1g is the second outermost of the seven TRAPPIST-1 planets
points: Outermost of the seven TRAPPIST-1 planets
Radius ~1.13× Earth
Receives less stellar energy than Mars
Possible icy surface or thin atmosphere
Important for understanding system dynamics

TRAPPIST-1b.explanation: TRAPPIST-1b was found by JWST to have no thick atmosphere making it a bare rock
points: Innermost planet of TRAPPIST-1 system
JWST observations (2023) showed no thick atmosphere
Likely bare rocky surface
Very hot dayside – extreme stellar irradiation
Tidally locked

GJ 876b.explanation: GJ 876b was the first gas giant exoplanet discovered around a red dwarf star
points: First gas giant found around red dwarf (1998)
Mass ~2.3 Jupiter masses
Orbital period ~61 days
Part of resonant multi-planet system
Helped understand planet formation around M dwarfs

51 Pegasi b.explanation: 51 Pegasi b was the first exoplanet discovered around a sun-like star in 1995
points: First exoplanet around main-sequence Sun-like star (1995)
Hot Jupiter – 4-day orbit
Mass ~0.47 Jupiter masses
Revolutionized exoplanet science – showed planets close to stars
Won Nobel Prize in Physics 2019 (Mayor & Queloz)

HD 209458b.explanation: HD 209458b also known as Osiris was the first exoplanet seen transiting its star
points: First transiting exoplanet (1999)
First atmosphere detected (sodium, hydrogen escape)
Hot Jupiter with evaporating atmosphere – comet-like tail
Named Osiris – losing mass like mythological figure
Radius inflated due to heat

TrES-1b.explanation: TrES-1b was the first exoplanet found using a small amateur-sized telescope network
points: First planet discovered by Trans-atlantic Exoplanet Survey (2004)
Hot Jupiter with 3-day orbit
Demonstrated small telescopes could find planets
Pioneered wide-field transit surveys
Mass ~0.76 Jupiter masses

HAT-P-1b.explanation: HAT-P-1b is a bloated hot Jupiter with an extremely low density for its size
points: One of the most inflated hot Jupiters
Radius ~1.38 Jupiter radii, mass ~0.45 Jupiter masses
Very low density – ~0.35 g/cm³
Orbiting bright star – easy to study
Helped understand planet inflation mechanisms

XO-1b.explanation: XO-1b is a hot Jupiter discovered using a small wide-field telescope in New Mexico
points: Discovered by XO Project – small telescope in Hawaii/New Mexico
Hot Jupiter with 3.94-day orbit
Mass ~0.9 Jupiter masses
Bright host star – good for follow-up
Early amateur-professional collaboration success

COROT-7b.explanation: CoRoT-7b was the first rocky exoplanet with a measured radius found outside our system
points: First confirmed rocky exoplanet (2009)
Radius ~1.58× Earth
Very close orbit – 0.85-day period
Surface temperature ~1,800–2,600 °C
Likely lava world

Kepler-10b.explanation: Kepler-10b was the first confirmed rocky planet found by the Kepler space telescope
points: First rocky planet confirmed by Kepler (2011)
Radius ~1.47× Earth, mass ~3.3–5.8 Earth masses
Very short orbit – 0.84 days
Extreme dayside temperature ~1,400 °C
Helped validate Kepler's small-planet detections

Kepler-11b.explanation: Kepler-11 has six transiting planets all crammed closer to their star than Earth is to the Sun
points: First system with six transiting planets
All six planets orbit closer than Mercury
Very compact system – demonstrates planet migration
Includes small rocky planets and mini-Neptunes
Important for understanding multi-planet dynamics

55 Cancri b.explanation: 55 Cancri b was one of the earliest known exoplanets around a sun-like star
points: One of the first hot Jupiters discovered (1996)
Mass ~0.83 Jupiter masses
Short orbit – 14.65 days
Part of one of the nearest multi-planet systems (~41 light-years)
Host star very bright – excellent for characterization

Tau Bootis b.explanation: Tau Bootis b is a massive hot Jupiter orbiting very close to its bright host star
points: Massive hot Jupiter ~5.9 Jupiter masses
Very short orbit – 3.31 days
Bright host star – early detection via radial velocity
Strongly irradiated – high temperature
Helped early understanding of hot Jupiter formation

70 Virginis b.explanation: 70 Virginis b was one of the first exoplanets found and initially called a Goldilocks planet
points: One of the first exoplanets discovered (1996)
Mass ~7.4 Jupiter masses
Wide orbit ~0.48 AU – more temperate than hot Jupiters
Early candidate for habitable conditions (before better data)
Orbiting G-type star

47 Ursae Majoris b.explanation: 47 Ursae Majoris b was one of the first Jupiter analogs found in a wide stable orbit
points: Jupiter-like planet in wide orbit ~2.1 AU
Mass ~2.5–4 Jupiter masses
Stable orbit around Sun-like star
Early example of Jupiter analog
Part of multi-planet system

Rho Coronae Borealis b.explanation: Rho CrB b was notable as one of the first hot Jupiters discovered in the 1990s
points: One of the first hot Jupiters (1997)
Mass ~1 Jupiter mass
Short orbit ~39.8 days
Orbiting bright G-type star
Helped establish hot Jupiter population

Kepler-47c.explanation: Kepler-47c orbits two stars in a stable circumbinary orbit in the habitable zone
points: First circumbinary planet in habitable zone
Gas giant ~4.6 Earth radii
Stable orbit around binary star pair
Receives Earth-like flux from two stars
Demonstrates habitable zone stability in binary systems

GJ 504b.explanation: GJ 504b is a directly imaged pink-magenta gas giant larger than Jupiter
points: One of the first directly imaged planets (2013)
Pink-magenta color – unusual for gas giants
Mass ~4–10 Jupiter masses
Very wide orbit ~44 AU
Still forming – young system

MOA-2007-BLG-192b.explanation: This super Earth orbits a tiny brown dwarf star and was found by gravitational microlensing
points: Super-Earth ~3.3 Earth masses
Orbits very low-mass brown dwarf / late M dwarf
Discovered via gravitational microlensing
Cold planet – far from host
Demonstrates microlensing sensitivity to low-mass hosts

OGLE-2016-BLG-1195Lb.explanation: This is one of the coldest known rocky exoplanets orbiting far from its host star
points: Earth-mass planet (~1.4 Earth masses)
Very cold – ~−223 °C (similar to Pluto)
Wide orbit ~2 AU around ultra-cool dwarf
Discovered via microlensing
One of the most distant and coldest rocky planets known

PSO J318.5-22.explanation: PSO J318 is a rogue gas giant drifting alone without a star about 80 light-years away
points: Rogue planet – no host star
Gas giant ~6 Jupiter masses
Very young – still glowing from formation heat
Temperature ~1,100 K
Drifting through space ~80 light-years away

Oph 11b.explanation: Ophiuchus 11b is one of the youngest directly imaged planets still glowing from formation heat
points: Very young gas giant (~1–3 million years old)
Still glowing strongly in infrared
Mass ~2–8 Jupiter masses
Wide orbit around brown dwarf pair
Helps understand early planet formation
